title: Binary Search Trees

sections.heading: ADT and Representation Invariant
sections.body:
A binary search tree (BST) stores a dynamic set of keys drawn from a totally ordered universe and supports SEARCH, INSERT, DELETE, MINIMUM, MAXIMUM, SUCCESSOR and PREDECESSOR. Each node holds a key, optional satellite data, and three pointers: `left`, `right`, `parent` (METU's CENG213/CENG315 slide deck reuses CLRS's second-edition bracket notation — `key[x]`, `left[x]`, `right[x]`, `p[x]` — rather than the fourth edition's dot notation `x.key`, `x.left`, `x.right`, `x.p`; the fields are identical either way).

The representation invariant — the **binary-search-tree property** — is a recursive statement about every node $x$:

$$y.\text{key} \le x.\text{key} \quad \text{for every node } y \text{ in the left subtree of } x$$

$$y.\text{key} \ge x.\text{key} \quad \text{for every node } y \text{ in the right subtree of } x$$

Two consequences drive every operation below. First, comparing the target key against key($x$) at any node tells you which subtree — if either — can contain it, which is what turns SEARCH into a single root-to-leaf walk instead of an exhaustive scan. Second, an inorder walk (left, node, right) visits keys in nondecreasing order; this is not a separate fact to remember, it is the invariant restated as a traversal order.

The $\le$/$\ge$ phrasing (rather than strict $<$/$>$) technically permits equal keys on either side. A correct implementation has to pick one side for ties and document it — this card sends equal keys right (`key < x.key` goes left, everything else goes right), so inserting a duplicate key always lands as the rightmost occurrence in an inorder walk of equal keys. `std::map`/`std::set` sidestep the question by rejecting duplicate keys outright; `std::multimap` keeps duplicates but guarantees their relative insertion order is preserved among equal keys.

sections.heading: Search, Minimum/Maximum and Successor
sections.body:
SEARCH($x$, $k$) starts at the root and, at each node, compares $k$ to key($x$): equal stops, smaller goes left, larger goes right; it terminates at the key or at a NULL pointer, doing one comparison per level, so its cost is $O(h)$ for a tree of height $h$. MINIMUM and MAXIMUM are the same idea specialized to always go one direction: MINIMUM follows `left` pointers until `left` is NULL, MAXIMUM follows `right` pointers until `right` is NULL — also $O(h)$.

SUCCESSOR($x$), the node whose key is the smallest key greater than key($x$), has two cases. If $x$ has a right subtree, the successor is MINIMUM(right($x$)) — the smallest key still guaranteed larger than key($x$). If $x$ has no right subtree, the successor is the lowest ancestor of $x$ whose left child is also an ancestor of $x$: walk up through parent pointers as long as you keep arriving from a right child; the first ancestor you reach by arriving from a left child is the successor (if the walk reaches the root without ever arriving from a left child, $x$ was the maximum and has no successor). PREDECESSOR is the mirror image.

These are exactly the operations CLRS's own example tree is built to illustrate, and METU's slides reuse that figure directly. Inserting 15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4, 13, 9 into an empty tree, in that order, gives a height-4 tree with MINIMUM $=2$, MAXIMUM $=20$, SUCCESSOR($15$) $=17$ (15's right subtree is rooted at 18, whose leftmost descendant is 17), and SUCCESSOR($13$) $=15$: 13 has no right child, so the walk goes 13 → 7 (13 is 7's right child, keep climbing) → 6 (7 is 6's right child, keep climbing) → 15 (6 is 15's *left* child — stop; 15 is the successor).

sections.heading: Insertion and Deletion via TRANSPLANT
sections.body:
INSERT($T$, $z$) reuses the SEARCH walk: starting at the root, follow `left`/`right` by comparing key($z$) at each node, remembering the last node visited ($y$), until falling off the tree; $z$ becomes $y$'s left or right child depending on the comparison, or the new root if the tree was empty. No restructuring happens — insertion only ever attaches a new leaf, so the BST property holds by construction (every comparison that led to the leaf's position is still true after it's attached).

Deletion is the operation that has to restructure the tree, and CLRS organizes it around a helper, TRANSPLANT($T$, $u$, $v$), that replaces the subtree rooted at $u$ with the subtree rooted at $v$ by rewriting exactly one pointer — $u$'s parent's child pointer — and $v$'s parent pointer if $v$ is not NULL. It never touches $v$'s own children, so the caller is responsible for reattaching them. DELETE($T$, $z$) has three cases:

- $z$ has no left child: `TRANSPLANT(T, z, right(z))` — $z$'s right subtree (possibly NULL) takes $z$'s place directly.
- $z$ has a left child but no right child: the mirror image, `TRANSPLANT(T, z, left(z))`.
- $z$ has two children: let $y = $ `MINIMUM(right(z))`, $z$'s inorder successor. $y$ has no left child (it is a minimum). If $y$ is not $z$'s immediate right child, $y$ is first spliced out of its current spot with `TRANSPLANT(T, y, right(y))`, then it inherits $z$'s whole right subtree (`y.right = z.right`, with the parent pointer fixed up). Either way, `TRANSPLANT(T, z, y)` then puts $y$ where $z$ was, and `y.left = z.left` gives $y$ z's left subtree.

The guard — "if $y$ is not $z$'s immediate right child" — is not cosmetic. Skipping it and always running the splice-out step happens to still work when $y$'s own right child is non-NULL, because a later unconditional pointer write overwrites the transient bad state. But if $y$ is z's immediate right child *and* is itself a leaf, the unconditional version reads $y$'s right pointer — now NULL — and dereferences it. Tested directly against the example tree: deleting node 18 (two children 17 and 20, where 20 is a leaf) with the unguarded version segfaults; the guarded version deletes it correctly.

sections.heading: Correctness and the Cost of Randomness
sections.body:
Every operation above preserves the BST property by induction: SEARCH/MINIMUM/MAXIMUM only read; INSERT attaches one new leaf whose position is consistent with the comparisons that found it; TRANSPLANT only ever replaces one subtree with another whose keys already satisfy the same bound relative to the rest of the tree (the successor $y$'s key lies strictly between key($z$) and every key in $z$'s right subtree, which is exactly why it's safe to drop $y$ into $z$'s place).

All costs above are $O(h)$, so the question is how large $h$ gets. In the worst case it is $\Theta(n)$: inserting already-sorted keys $1, 2, \dots, n$ never puts anything in a left subtree, producing a right-only chain of height $n-1$ — the same key set that Figure 12.1 in CLRS shows can also form a height-2 tree, depending only on insertion order.

For a tree built by inserting $n$ distinct keys in *uniformly random* order, the expected shape is close to balanced. The classic argument: two keys $x < y$ end up as ancestor/descendant (equivalently, compared against each other during construction) iff one of them is the first, among all keys between $x$ and $y$ inclusive, to be inserted — exactly the same event that makes quicksort compare two elements when one is picked as a pivot before any element between them. This identifies the internal path length of a randomly built BST with the comparison count of randomized quicksort, giving the recurrence:

$$I(n) = (n - 1) + \frac{2}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} I(k)$$

whose solution is $I(n) = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number — $\Theta(n \lg n)$, so the *average* node depth $I(n)/n$ is $2\ln n - \Theta(1)$. Checked numerically for $n = 1000$: $I(n)/n \approx 10.99$, versus $9$, the minimum possible height for 1000 nodes — a randomly built BST is close to balanced on average, but this says nothing about the *worst-case height*, which a separate, harder argument (CLRS's exponential-height technique, bounding $E[2^{X_n}]$ and applying Jensen's inequality) shows is also $O(\lg n)$ in expectation. Neither result bounds the height of a tree built from adversarial or already-sorted input — that is exactly the gap self-balancing trees close.

sections.heading: Variants and Engineering Trade-offs
sections.body:
A plain BST gives no worst-case guarantee, so production structures add balancing on top of the same SEARCH/INSERT/DELETE skeleton. AVL trees bound $|height(left) - height(right)| \le 1$ at every node; red-black trees relax that to a color invariant guaranteeing height $\le 2\lg(n+1)$. Both restore their invariant after INSERT/DELETE using the same primitive, a rotation (LEFT-ROTATE/RIGHT-ROTATE), which changes a constant number of pointers and preserves the BST property — the METU slide set introduces rotations right alongside the plain-BST chapter for exactly this reason. Treaps take a different route: each node also carries a random priority, and the tree is kept heap-ordered on priority via rotations, which makes the *expected* shape provably as balanced as a randomly built BST regardless of insertion order, without any explicit rebalancing rule.

Memory layout matters as much as the asymptotics. Every operation is a chain of pointer dereferences (`left`, `right`, and often `parent`), and consecutively visited nodes are rarely adjacent in memory, so a BST walk of height $h$ can cost up to $h$ cache misses — this is why B-trees, which fan out to match a cache line or disk block instead of branching two-way, dominate for on-disk or hierarchical-memory indexes. Storing `parent` costs one pointer per node purely to make SUCCESSOR/PREDECESSOR and deletion simple; iterative in-order traversal can drop it entirely using an explicit stack, or with no extra space at all via Morris traversal, which temporarily threads `right` pointers to inorder successors instead of recursing.

code.caption: CLRS-style BST: insert, search, TRANSPLANT-based delete, inorder traversal (verified against Figure 12.1/12.2's example tree with gcc-15 -Wall -Wextra).

worked_example.problem: Starting from an empty tree, insert the keys 15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4, 13, 9 in that order (CLRS's own Figure 12.1/12.2 example). Then, from that same 11-node tree, trace two independent deletions: (a) delete key 6, whose two children are 3's subtree and the leaf-adjacent node 7; (b) delete the root, key 15. Give the TRANSPLANT calls and the resulting inorder sequence for each.
worked_example.solution:
**Build.** Inserting in the given order produces a tree of height 4 with root 15; left subtree rooted at 6 (children 3 and 7; 3's children are 2 and 4; 7's right child is 13, whose left child is 9); right subtree rooted at 18 (children 17 and 20). Sorted inorder listing: `2 3 4 6 7 9 13 15 17 18 20`. This was checked by compiling and running the listing above with `gcc-15 -Wall -Wextra`.

**(a) Delete 6 (`z = 6`, `z.left = 3`-subtree, `z.right = 7`-subtree).** `y = MINIMUM(z.right) = MINIMUM(7) = 7` itself, since 7 has no left child. Because `y.parent == z` (7 is 6's direct right child), the splice-out step is skipped: go straight to `TRANSPLANT(T, 6, 7)` — 15's left pointer now points at 7, and 7's parent becomes 15. Finally `y.left = z.left`: 7's left pointer becomes the 3-subtree, and 3's parent becomes 7. Node 7 keeps its own right subtree (13, with 9 under it) untouched throughout. Result: `2 3 4 7 9 13 15 17 18 20`.

**(b) Delete 15, the root (`z = 15`, `z.left = 6`-subtree, `z.right = 18`-subtree).** `y = MINIMUM(z.right) = MINIMUM(18) = 17`, since 18's left child 17 has no left child of its own. Here `y.parent = 18 \ne z`, so both steps run: first `TRANSPLANT(T, 17, right(17))` — 17 has no right child, so this sets 18's left pointer to NULL, detaching 17 from its old spot; then `y.right = z.right` gives 17 the 18-subtree (18, with 20 as its only remaining child; 18's parent becomes 17). Next `TRANSPLANT(T, 15, 17)` makes 17 the new root. Finally `y.left = z.left` gives 17 the 6-subtree (6's parent becomes 17). Result: new root is 17, inorder `2 3 4 6 7 9 13 17 18 20`.

Both traces were checked against the compiled program's actual output, not just worked by hand.

pitfalls: Omitting the `y.parent != z` guard in two-children deletion. It looks harmless (a later pointer write papers over the bad intermediate state whenever the successor has its own right child), but when the successor is z's immediate right child *and* is itself a leaf, the unguarded code dereferences a NULL right pointer. Reproduced directly: deleting node 18 (children 17 and the leaf 20) from the example tree segfaults without the guard.

Treating $O(\lg n)$ as a guarantee rather than an expectation over random insertion order. Inserting already-sorted or reverse-sorted data degrades a plain BST to a $\Theta(n)$-height chain; any code path that can receive sorted input (loading a pre-sorted log file, replaying an index) needs a self-balancing variant.

Forgetting that TRANSPLANT does not touch the moved subtree's own children. Calling it and then failing to reattach `v`'s former children (or reattaching them to the wrong side) silently breaks the BST property in a way that inorder traversal may still print as "sorted" if the corruption only affects parent pointers, not key order — always validate parent pointers separately from key order when testing a deletion implementation.

Recursive inorder traversal assumes $O(h)$ stack space; on a degenerate $\Theta(n)$-height chain this is $\Theta(n)$ stack frames, which can overflow the stack for large $n$ where an $O(1)$-space Morris traversal or an explicit heap-allocated stack would not.

Confusing the BST property with the heap property: a BST orders *along* root-to-leaf paths (every left descendant $\le$ every ancestor $\le$ every right descendant), while a binary heap only orders parent against immediate children — a valid max-heap array is not, in general, a valid BST inorder sequence, and vice versa.
applications: C++ `std::map`/`std::set`: a self-balancing (red-black) BST; ordered iteration and `lower_bound`/`upper_bound` rely directly on the inorder-is-sorted property described above.
`java.util.TreeMap`/`TreeSet`: same idea, red-black tree under a BST interface, chosen over a hash table specifically to keep keys iterable in sorted order.

Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler): keeps the runnable-task run queue in a red-black tree keyed by virtual runtime, so "pick the next task to run" is a MINIMUM call and "task consumed its slice" is a DELETE+INSERT with a new key.

glibc's POSIX `tsearch`/`tfind`/`tdelete` (`<search.h>`): a generic, unbalanced BST exposed as a C library primitive — a real-world instance of the plain, non-self-balancing structure this card describes, with the corresponding risk of $\Theta(n)$ behavior on sorted input.

Compilers and interpreters: expression trees and simple symbol tables are natural unbalanced BSTs when key order is close to random (e.g. hashed or randomly-generated identifiers); inorder traversal reconstructs an infix expression directly from the tree shape.
exam_focus: METU's CENG213/CENG315 slide deck reuses CLRS's second-edition figures verbatim for this topic (Figures 12.1–12.2 for the BST property and queries, 12.4 for deletion cases, 13.2 for rotations), so the course follows CLRS's bracket field notation — `key[x]`, `left[x]`, `right[x]`, `p[x]` — rather than the newer dot notation; use that notation on a METU exam unless the exam sheet says otherwise.

The rotation figure (LEFT-ROTATE/RIGHT-ROTATE, Figure 13.2) is presented immediately alongside the plain-BST chapter in the slide set, which signals the course's sequencing: plain BST operations first, rotations as the shared primitive for the balanced trees (AVL/red-black) that follow.

self_check.question: Why does an inorder traversal of a binary search tree always output keys in nondecreasing order, and what does that imply about testing a BST implementation?
self_check.answer: By induction on subtree size: the BST property says every key in $x$'s left subtree is $\le$ key($x$) and every key in $x$'s right subtree is $\ge$ key($x$); inorder recursion visits left, then $x$, then right, so by the inductive hypothesis it prints the (sorted) left subtree, then key($x$) — which is $\ge$ everything just printed — then the (sorted) right subtree, whose smallest element is $\ge$ key($x$). Base case (empty subtree) prints nothing, trivially sorted. Implication for testing: checking that inorder traversal output is sorted is a *necessary but not sufficient* correctness check — it depends only on `left`/`right` pointers, so a deletion bug that corrupts `parent` pointers (breaking SUCCESSOR or a later deletion) can pass this check silently; parent-pointer consistency must be validated separately, as shown by the segfault case in the pitfalls list, which still prints a sorted inorder sequence right up until the crash.

self_check.question: A BST is built by inserting 1000 distinct keys in uniformly random order. Using the closed-form average node depth $I(n)/n = 2(n+1)H_n/n - 4$, estimate the average depth, and compare it to 9, the minimum possible height of any binary tree on 1000 nodes. What does the comparison say about why self-balancing trees are still needed?
self_check.answer: $H_{1000} \approx 7.485$, so $I(1000)/1000 = 2 \times 1001 \times 7.485/1000 - 4 \approx 14.986 - 4 = 10.99$. That is only about $1.22\times$ the optimal height of 9 — on *average*, a randomly built BST is already close to balanced, and rebalancing would buy little for random-order workloads. Self-balancing trees are still needed because this 10.99 figure is an *average over random insertion orders*; it says nothing about a specific, possibly adversarial or already-sorted, input sequence, for which the same 1000 keys build a height-999 chain. Guaranteeing $O(\lg n)$ height for *every* input, not just typical ones, is exactly the property AVL/red-black trees add on top of the plain BST.

self_check.question: Trace `DELETE` on a node $z$ that has two children where the inorder successor $y$ is *not* $z$'s immediate right child. Why does this case need two `TRANSPLANT` calls, while the case where $y$ is $z$'s immediate right child needs only one?
self_check.answer: Example from the worked example: deleting root 15 (children 6 and 18) where $y = $ MINIMUM(18) $= 17 \ne$ 18 $=$ `z.right`. Two things must happen: (1) $y$ has to be removed from its current position — `TRANSPLANT(T, y, right(y))` replaces $y$ in place with its own right subtree (here, NULL, since 17 has no right child), then `y.right = z.right` gives $y$ the *entire* subtree that used to be `z.right` (here, node 18 with its remaining child 20); (2) $y$ has to be installed where $z$ was — `TRANSPLANT(T, z, y)` plus `y.left = z.left`. Two `TRANSPLANT` calls because $y$ moves *twice*: out of its old spot, then into $z$'s spot. When $y$ *is* `z.right` directly, step (1) is unnecessary because $y$'s "old spot" and "the position it needs to inherit `z.right`'s subtree into" are the same node — $y$ already sits exactly where it needs to be relative to its own children, so it only has to move once, straight into $z$'s spot, which is why only `TRANSPLANT(T, z, y)` plus `y.left = z.left` are needed.

key_points: BST property: every left-subtree key ≤ node key ≤ every right-subtree key, applied recursively
Inorder traversal of a BST always yields sorted order — a restatement of the invariant, not a new fact
All core operations cost O(h): O(lg n) expected on random insertion order, O(n) on a degenerate chain
TRANSPLANT swaps one subtree for another by rewriting a single parent pointer; DELETE composes 2–3 calls
Two-children deletion needs the successor's y.parent ≠ z guard, or it can null-deref on a leaf successor
A plain BST gives no worst-case height guarantee — that's what AVL/red-black/treap variants add
tagline: A BST turns SEARCH into a root-to-leaf walk — O(lg n) on random input, O(n) on sorted input, hence self-balancing variants in practice.
tldr: A binary search tree keeps every left-subtree key $\le$ a node's key $\le$ every right-subtree key, which makes SEARCH/INSERT/DELETE all $O(h)$ walks and inorder traversal automatically sorted. Deletion is built from a single primitive, TRANSPLANT, composed 1–2 times depending on whether the node has 0, 1, or 2 children — the two-children case needs a guard against a real NULL-pointer bug, reproduced here directly. Height is $O(\lg n)$ in expectation over random insertion order but unbounded in the worst case, which is exactly the gap that AVL trees, red-black trees and treaps close.
